name: Rotoscope
basis: why: tracing each frame by hand keeps few tones and a firm line, and redrawing makes it boil; how: flat bands, wandering edges, new drawing on twos
note: Animation method, now often digital; boil is temporal.

lumenary.blurb: Traced by hand, frame by frame, as in A Scanner Darkly. Each drawing has its own few flat tones and its own shaky ink line, and the colour never quite stays inside the lines. On video a new drawing is made every second frame; on a still picture it keeps being redrawn, so the lines boil.

facts.bestOn: Video of people and faces; pictures with clear shapes

why: Tracing a photograph by hand loses most of its detail and keeps what the artist thought mattered: a few flat tones and a firm line. Because the tracing is redone for every frame, nothing lines up exactly from one drawing to the next, and the edges shiver. That shiver, called boil, is what makes a rotoscoped film feel hand-made and a little dreamlike even when the movement underneath is perfectly real.
how: Blur the frame slightly and cut its brightness into a few flat bands, keeping each pixel’s own colour.
Let the edges of the bands wander with noise that is new for every drawing.
Find the ink line where the brightness changes quickly, and thicken it.
Nudge the line and the colour by two different smooth random fields, so the colour slips out of the lines.
Make a fresh drawing only every second frame, on twos, and hold it in between.
history: The rotoscope was patented in 1917 by Max Fleischer, who had filmed his brother Dave in a clown suit and traced the frames to make Koko the Clown. Disney studied live-action film for Snow White (1937). In 1978 Ralph Bakshi made The Lord of the Rings largely over live action, and in 2001 Richard Linklater’s Waking Life used a computer to paint over video, a method refined for A Scanner Darkly (2006). Because every frame is drawn again, boil comes with the method, and is now often added on purpose.
uses: Turning phone video into a painted clip
terms: The shimmer of lines and edges that appears when every frame is drawn separately.
Drawing one new picture for every two frames of film, which is 12 drawings a second at 24 frames.
Reduce a continuous range of tones to a few flat levels.
paragraphs: The fill is a posterisation of a blurred copy of the frame. With brightness l from 0 to 1, after a blur of about 2.2 pixels at 640 wide, the band is chosen from l' = l + 0.14 b (nu - 1/2), where nu is value noise that changes with the drawing number and b is the boil slider. The tones are n bands of width 1/n; the pixel keeps its own colour, scaled so that its brightness becomes the middle of its band, q/l, then pushed away from grey by a saturation factor of 0.75 to 1.65 and mixed with the blurred original by the wash slider.

The ink is the Sobel gradient magnitude of the brightness passed through a smoothstep from a to 1.7a, where a falls from 0.34 to 0.09 as the line slider rises; above half strength the line is thickened with a blur and a second threshold. Two smooth random fields, each value noise on a grid of 8 pixels and read back bilinearly, are renewed for every drawing and say how far to shift each pixel: one, up to 2.4 px times the boil, for the ink, and a different one, up to 5.5 px times the slip, for the colour. Because they differ, the fill and the line drift against each other. A new drawing is made every 1/24 s times 1, 2 or 3; in between, the last drawing is shown unchanged, which is the twos of animation.

equations.note: Posterising: l is the brightness, n the number of tones, b the boil slider and nu value noise renewed for every drawing.
The ink line: the gradient is a Sobel filter and L is the line slider (0 to 1).

equations.tex: \mathbf C_{\text{out}}=(1-m)\,\mathbf C(\mathbf p+\mathbf d_C)+m\,\mathbf C_{\text{ink}},\qquad m=m(\mathbf p+\mathbf d_L)
equations.note: The colour and the ink are read at different shifts, so they never agree exactly.

presets.text: Three tones, a firm line and plenty of boil give a graphic-novel look.
Soft washed colour and little line looks like paint laid over film.
A new drawing only every third frame makes the boil slow and jerky.
